title: Scalar and vector projection
section: Analytic Geometry of R3 ▷ The Dot Product
terms: scalar projection; vector projection; orthogonal decomposition.

exposition.text:
For a ̸= 0, the scalar projection of b onto the directed vector a is (a · b)/∥a∥; it can be negative.
The vector projection is proj b = (a · b)a/(a · a). Thus b splits uniquely as a component parallel
a
to a plus a component perpendicular to a.
Projection solves a nearest-point problem: the point ta closest to b has t = (a · b)/(a · a).

affine line, first subtract a point on that line. Do not confuse a signed scalar projection with the
nonnegative length of a projected vector.
Reflection across a line through the origin preserves the parallel component and reverses the
perpendicular component, so it maps b to 2 proj b − b. Reversing the chosen direction of the line

question.text:
Let L be the line spanned by (1, 2, 2). Reflection across L keeps the component parallel to L
and negates the perpendicular component. What is the image of (3, 0, 0)?
(A) (−7/3, 4/3, 4/3) (B) (1/3, 2/3, 2/3)
(C) (−3, 0, 0) (D) (7/3, −4/3, −4/3)
(E) (1, 2, 2)

solution.text:
The parallel component is p = [3/9](1, 2, 2) = (1/3, 2/3, 2/3). Reflection sends b = p + (b − p)
to p − (b − p) = 2p − b = (−7/3, 4/3, 4/3). Its squared norm remains 9, providing a check.
